metadata.title: When Should You Update the Handbook?
metadata.purpose: Answer what actually triggers the need to update an employee handbook -- a date on the calendar, or a change in the law. Lands the carry-out that updates should be tracked by the law that triggers them, not a scheduled review.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible handbook-maintenance account from the title/family rather than lifting facts that were never written.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (a spring paid-leave minimum increase that touches exactly the leave-policy section, then fills in with a dated amendment record)

beats.narration_text: Someone at a company asks when they should update the employee handbook. The wrong first answer is a date on the calendar. Liam is here to take them through the real trigger.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What updates the handbook -- the calendar?', hesitates on 'calendar', corrects to 'law', lands the real question

props.text:
What updates
the handbook —
the calendar?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('calendar' -> 'law') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The obvious plan is a yearly review -- read the whole handbook every December, fix what looks stale. But a law that changes in March doesn't wait for December. The section it touches is wrong the day the law takes effect, and it stays wrong for however many months are left until the scheduled read-through.

shot.new_visual_element: A calendar with one marked review day in December; a law-change icon lighting up in March, far from the marked day, with the handbook page beside it flipping to a struck-through 'current'

production_viz.label: The calendar review, and the gap it leaves
production_viz.mechanic: A year-strip calendar with one day in December ringed and labelled 'REVIEW'. A law-change glyph lights up in March, far from the ringed day. Beside it, a handbook page reading 'current' flips to a struck-through 'current' the instant the glyph lights, while the ringed December day stays untouched and far away.

beats.narration_text: The fix isn't reviewing more often -- it's tracking updates by what actually triggers them: a specific legal change. Watch the anchor: a state raises its paid-leave minimum in the spring. That one change touches exactly one section -- the leave policy -- not the whole handbook.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a single law-change event connecting by a line to one highlighted handbook section, the rest of the handbook dimmed

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one law change, one section
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A law-change card reading 'paid-leave minimum raised' appears at left. A thin line draws from it to a single highlighted row in a stacked list of handbook sections labelled 'LEAVE POLICY'; every other section in the stack stays dim and untouched. THIS EXACT SECTION ROW RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That section gets a specific fix -- new language for the new minimum -- logged with what changed, why, and the date it took effect, so there's a record instead of a silent overwrite. But a flagged section isn't a finished one; the drafted language still needs a legal read before it ships. And a quiet quarter with no flags doesn't mean the handbook is complete -- it means no tracked law changed, which isn't the same thing.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the leave section fills with a dated amendment entry, then splits into 'flagged is not final' and 'quiet is not complete'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- logged, not finished
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 LEAVE POLICY ROW RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in with an amendment entry (what changed / why / effective date) one line at a time, then slides into a small dated log. It splits into two cards: left reads 'section: flagged' with a struck-through 'DONE' beneath it labelled 'flagged is not final'; right reads 'quarter: no flags' with a faint new law-change card appearing at its edge labelled 'quiet is not complete'.

beats.narration_text: A handbook doesn't go out of date on a birthday -- it goes out of date the day a law changes. Track updates by the law that triggers them, not a date on the calendar.

props.quote: A handbook doesn't go out of date on a birthday -- it goes out of date the day a law changes. Track updates by the law that triggers them, not a date on the calendar.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt -- read it with me. Pick one policy in your employee handbook -- leave, overtime, remote work, anything. Write down the date it was last actually changed, and find out whether any law touching that topic has changed since. If you can't answer either question, that's the gap this whole habit is meant to close. Liam, in for Bear.
